lesson.subtitle: Lesson 10 -- Speaking Under Pressure
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Denise Gadelha Rocha | Lesson 10 -- Speaking Under Pressure
lesson.grammar_point: used to, be used to and get used to

listenings.text: There is a sentence I hear from every senior person who works in a second language, and it is always the same sentence. In my own language I am a director, and in English I sound like somebody's assistant. That is not vanity. It is accurate, and it is not about grammar. Authority in a meeting is carried almost entirely by delivery, by pace, by where the pauses fall, by whether you finish your own sentences. In a second language all of that goes first, long before the vocabulary does. The word arrives late, the sentence trails off, and the room quietly gives the floor to somebody else. Nobody decides to do it. It simply happens. So what I tell people is to stop trying to be faster. Speed is not the thing you lost. Work on holding the floor while you are slow, because that is the part the room is actually reading.

For years I had one move when a word did not come, and it was to apologise. Sorry, my English. I said it perhaps four times a call, and I thought it was modesty. It was not. Every one of those apologies told the room to lower its expectations of me, and rooms do what they are told. What I have now is three sentences and nothing else. Let me put that a different way. The short answer is yes, and I will come back to the detail. And, when I genuinely have nothing, that is a fair question, give me a second on it. I used to think a phrase like that was filler. It is not filler, it is furniture. It holds the space up while I find the word. And the Spanish still arrives first, most days. It just does not get to finish the sentence any more.

extra_audio.text: Let me put that a different way. The short answer is yes, and I will come back to the detail. That is a fair question. Give me a second on it. I do not have that number in front of me. I will send it today.

reading.rtitle: Observation Notes -- Regional Commercial Review, 90 Minutes
paras: The director under observation is not short of English. In ninety minutes she used every structure the role requires, and twice she corrected the group on a technical point. What she is short of is a way back. Three times a word failed to arrive on time, and all three times the sentence trailed off and somebody else took the floor.

This is worth stating precisely, because she will not state it kindly herself. The word did not disappear; it arrived about four seconds late. Four things were queueing for the same second: the Spanish she had been speaking all morning, the grammar she was monitoring, the argument she was tracking, and the word itself. In her first language that queue does not exist. She used to read the delay as evidence that her English had gone backwards. It is evidence of load, and of nothing else.

So the work here is not prevention. It is recovery. She is not used to speaking while she searches, because in her own language she has never had to. Those four seconds have to be filled with something other than an apology, and sorry, my English is the one filler that costs authority every single time it is used. A rephrase, a placeholder phrase, or a deliberate pause with the eyes up: each buys the same time, and each reads as poise rather than as a gap.

She is already getting used to the pause. Twice in the second hour she stalled on purpose, held the floor and finished the point, and her delivery in both cases was indistinguishable from her delivery in her first language. That is the whole change. It is worth adding that nobody else in that call could have told you which of her sentences arrived late.
